summary: Defines a simple challenge-response way to log in to IMAP mail servers, and the same idea works for POP. The server sends a changing challenge and the client proves it knows the password without sending the password itself. It replaces RFC 2095.

plainLanguage.summary: CRAM-MD5 lets a mail client prove it knows a shared secret without sending that secret as a password. The server checks a digest based on a challenge, but this method does not protect the rest of the connection.

questions: how does challenge response authentication work for imap
how is the cram-md5 digest calculated
subtitle: Defines CRAM-MD5 challenge-response authentication for IMAP and possible POP3 use.

tldr.problem: IMAP lacked a lightweight alternative to sending a reusable cleartext password, while some existing challenge-response methods required the server to store the shared secret in cleartext.
tldr.mechanism: The server sends a challenge containing a timestamp; the client returns its user name and a keyed-MD5 digest of that timestamp using a shared secret.
tldr.outcome: CRAM-MD5 avoids sending the password itself and can avoid storing the secret in cleartext, but it provides no protection mechanism and remains vulnerable to active attacks.

today: RFC 2195 is listed as a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 2095, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: A Challenge-Response Alternative
sections.content:
IMAP already had stronger authentication mechanisms, but they required supporting security infrastructure. Its simpler LOGIN command used a user name and password, while the POP3 APOP mechanism required both client and server to access the shared secret in cleartext.

This memo defines a simple challenge-response method that uses a keyed MD5 digest and can be used with IMAP and, in principle, POP3.
sections.plainLanguage: The method aims to avoid sending a reusable password and avoid storing the shared secret directly on the server. It uses a challenge and a calculated response instead.

sections.title: How CRAM-MD5 Works
sections.content:
The server sends a challenge containing a string of random digits, a timestamp, and its fully qualified host name. The client computes a keyed-MD5 digest of the timestamp using the shared secret.

The client returns its user name, a space, and the digest as 16 octets written in lowercase hexadecimal. The server checks the digest and, if it is correct, should treat the client as authenticated.
sections.plainLanguage: The server sends a challenge, and the client uses the shared secret to calculate a response. The server authenticates the client if the returned digest matches its own calculation.

sections.title: What the Mechanism Does Not Protect
sections.content:
CRAM does not provide a protection mechanism for the connection. The memo says it is believed to provide origin identification and replay protection for a session, but users remain vulnerable to active attacks such as TCP session hijacking.

Storing precomputed contexts is only marginally better than storing the shared secret in cleartext if the server itself is compromised. Servers must protect these stored values according to the value of the mailboxes and identities.
sections.plainLanguage: CRAM-MD5 checks authentication but does not encrypt or protect all connection data. A compromised server or an active attacker can still create serious risks.
